opening.headline: Problems where the output format is different every time and cannot be used in subsequent work are solved with examples, formatting, and positive instructions.
body: If the content is correct but the appearance is different every time and a person has to reorganize it, the assistant has not become part of the follow-up work. I'm trying to transfer the order information to the inventory sheet, but it's a struggle every time I come back to a list yesterday and a paragraph today.

This lesson covers three tools to communicate the look you want to your assistant. These are direct examples of shapes, output formats that specify items and their order, and positive instructions that change prohibitions into things to do. At the end, we solve the case of fixing the output form of the order reception assistant.

Customer name | Item | Quantity | Delivery date

paragraphs: The order reception assistant organizes orders received via text message. But Monday's response is a list of numbers, Tuesday's is a paragraph, and Wednesday's is a table. In some answers the quantity is in parentheses, in others it is in the sentence.
Transferring it to an inventory sheet requires a person to format it and reorganize it each time. The content is correct, but the shape is shaky and subsequent work is interrupted.
The question for this class is this. How should I write the format so that the assistant answers in the same format?

screens.outro: Let me first think about your experience.

screens.title: Have you ever had to rearrange the result format because it was unstable?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit anything, so think about it first before clicking.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to receive a ticket, but the paragraph came back and you made the ticket yourself?
items.answer: It's a common experience. At this time, even though the phrase “organize it in a table” was likely there, there were no column names or order. The word table alone does not determine which columns to put in and in which order.

items.prompt: Have you ever written, “Don’t write like this,” but ended up doing it that way more often?
items.answer: Prohibition sentences only tell you what you shouldn't do, not what you should do. If the assistant fills in the blank spaces with guesswork, an unwanted shape may appear. In this lesson we will look at solutions.

items.prompt: Which worked better: explaining the format verbally or showing the shape in person?
items.answer: In general, things that show the shape directly work better. Explanations leave room for interpretation, but examples provide a visual guide. It is most reliable if you add examples to your explanation.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start with the most direct way to show what it looks like: an example.

screens.title: Example: The shape of one case determines the shape of several cases
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow how the response takes shape as examples are added one by one to the instructions.

visual.alt: Illustration showing how the example blocks on the right are inserted one by one into the draft instructions on the left.

steps.title: What Examples Do
steps.body: Claude Prompt Guide introduces examples as one of the most reliable ways to guide output format, tone, and structure. GPT guidance also recommends that the guidance include short examples of acceptable and unacceptable output. The visual appearance is more evident as a reference than the format described in words.

steps.title: Three conditions for a good example
steps.body: The first is relevance. You must use input that resembles order text received in actual work. Second is diversity. In addition to normal orders, you should include boundary cases such as missing characters in the customer name. Third is structuring. Be sure to separate examples from instructional sentences.

steps.title: How to distinguish examples from instructions
steps.body: Claude's instructions recommend wrapping examples with the tag `<example>` to separate them from the instructions, and grouping multiple examples with `<examples>`. Tags provide clear boundaries so your Assistant doesn't misunderstand sentences in the examples as new instructions.

steps.title: Problems that occur when only one entry is entered
steps.body: With just one example, it's easy for the assistant to follow not only the look but also the content. If our example contains 200 ballpoint pens, other orders may contain pens or similar quantities. To prevent this, show two or three different spells. When comparing different guns, the only thing they have in common is their shape.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: The saying that the shape of one case determines the shape of ten cases is a double-edged sword. Since the content is easy to follow as the shape is well fixed, the rule is to write two or three examples with relevance, variety, and structure.

screens.outro: If the shape is shown as an example, the following is an output format that specifies the items and order in writing.

screens.title: Output format: set rules for items, order, and spaces
screens.lead: Please read example instructions below. If you select a line range from the description on the right, you can see what that line does and what symptoms occur when it is missing.

data.code:
You are an assistant that reads order messages and consolidates them into a receipt form.

When one order message is entered, only the five-column table below is printed.
Order by: Customer Name | Item | Quantity | Delivery Date | Requires Verification
No explanatory sentences are written outside the table.
For values not present in the text, do not fill them in arbitrarily; instead, write "Pending verification" in the field.

<examples>
<example>
Input: Mr. Kim, Deputy at Hanbit Company. Please deliver 200 ballpoint pens by next Tuesday.
Output:
| Customer Name | Item | Quantity | Delivery Date | Confirmation Required |
| Hanbit Company | Ballpoint Pen | 200 units | Next Tuesday | Out of stock |
</example>
<example>
Input: Send me 50 notebooks and 30 files. I'm in a hurry.
Output:
| Customer Name | Item | Quantity | Delivery Date | Confirmation Required |
| To be verified | Note, file | 50 volumes, 30 items | To be verified | Customer name, delivery date |
</example>
</examples>

notes.note: Assign roles in one line. Gemini Gem guidance tells us to think of guidance in four areas: persona, task, context, and format. Without roles, you're left guessing what the assistant does, which falters the writing style and scope.

This is the key to the output format. Decide what items to include in the response, their order, and how to divide them. If the column order is missing, some days have the quantity before and some days after, it cannot be pasted into the sheet. The response “I do not write descriptive sentences outside the table” leaves only the table.

This is a blank space rule that determines what to use when there is no value. Without this line, the assistant will either fill in the blanks with random values ​​or skip the cells altogether, resulting in misaligned columns.

This is an example of two different inputs and outputs paired together. One is a normal order with all the values, and the other is an order missing the customer name and delivery date, so we are dealing with a borderline case. If there is only one case, symptoms will appear that even follow the content.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to format it, let's move on to how to write prohibitions.

screens.title: Prohibitions and positive instructions: say what you should do
screens.lead: Use the switch to go back and forth between prohibitive and positive sentences and compare how the same request is conveyed differently.

states.label: Forbidden type
states.body: These are sentences that only list what not to do, such as “Do not use explanatory sentences” or “Do not use Markdown.” Inhibitions don't tell you what to write, so your assistant guesses and fills in the blank spaces. I told them to leave out the description, but a single line greeting was added before and after the table, or I told them to leave out the markdown, but the list changed to unnumbered lines. GPT guidance also explains that positive, specific instructions to do this should be given priority over a long list of prohibitions. The longer the ban list, the greater the potential for conflict. For example, if there is a prohibition on not writing an explanation and a prohibition on giving reasons for unknown values ​​in the same guideline, it becomes unclear which one to follow.

states.label: positive type
states.body: This is a sentence rewritten to make the same request. For example, replace “Do not write descriptive sentences” with “Print only five columns of tables.” An example of Claude's guidance is to not write Markdown, but instead to write answers in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs. Affirmative forms reduce guessing by directly determining the shape of the response. When writing, read each prohibition sentence and ask what it tells you to do. In many cases, ten lines of prohibitive instructions can be replaced with three lines of positive instructions. If a ban is absolutely necessary, add a line explaining why. Knowing your why better reflects your intentions. Claude's instructions also explain that the closer the format of the prompts to the desired output format, the easier it is to follow.

screens.outro: Now let’s compare the before and after results of applying these principles all at once.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparison of responses before and after adding format instructions
screens.lead: Go back and forth between the before and after switches and see how the responses to the same three text orders change.

states.label: Before: No format instructions
states.body: When I entered the same order text three times, there were three different responses. The first is a list of numbers, the second is a paragraph with quantities written in sentences, and the third is a table with different column names. Everything is correct, but none of the responses can be pasted into the sheet. Since people have to edit each of the three responses in a different way, the time it takes to organize them increases as the number of orders increases. The instructions had just one line: “Keep your order neat and tidy.” The word neat is interpreted differently by each person, so its appearance is not fixed. In the absence of formatting instructions, the assistant picks a new likely shape each time, so the problem is not that the answers are wrong, but that they are inconsistent.

states.label: After: With format instructions
states.body: I've revised the instructions in three steps: In step 1, five items were written down in instructions and the field names were fixed. In Step 2, one completed order was entered as `<example>` to display its appearance. In step 3, “Do not write explanatory sentences outside the table” was changed to “Print only the table.” Then all three returned to the same five columns and could be pasted onto the sheet. Because the column names are fixed, the columns on the sheet and the columns in the response match one to one, and the task of moving things by hand has been reduced to copying and pasting. The success criterion for type instruction is to repeatedly check whether the same shape appears in the same input.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the before and after differences, let's follow the process of assembling the entire set of instructions into four sections.

screens.title: Description: Fix the output format of the order reception assistant.
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the instructions as they are completed in four sections. Pay attention to what shaking each zone prevents.

steps.title: role section
steps.body: First, write in one line, “Assistant who reads order letters and compiles them into intake forms.” If your role is clear, your assistant won't clean up text greetings or greetings.

steps.title: format area
steps.body: Next, write customer name, item, quantity, delivery date, and confirmation required to be printed in a table in this order. Item names and order are fixed, eliminating the problem of columns changing from day to day.

steps.title: Example area
steps.body: It shows two different input and output pairs. Select one order with all information and one order missing customer name and delivery date. Separating examples from instructions by enclosing them with `<examples>` will reduce the chances of items in the examples being copied to other orders.

steps.title: Blank rule area
steps.body: Finally, for unknown values, write “confirmation required” and state that they will not be populated arbitrarily. With this rule, the assistant will not make up a delivery date that is not in the text, and the table will reveal the fields that a person needs to check.

steps.title: Check with preview
steps.body: Before saving your instructions, try Previewing a few spells to see if they hold their appearance. Try placing normal orders, orders with missing information, and orders with multiple items. Each tool has a different name, but the Gem help also tells you that you must preview it and then click Save to save it. If you find an input that looks shaky in the preview, the quickest way to fix it is to add that input as a new example.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen how the four sections fit together, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class. As you read, think about how you might correct the wavering responses you initially saw.

paragraphs: The first question was how to write the format so the assistant would answer in the same format. The answer is to show the form in which something should be done rather than telling it not to be done. Direct examples of shapes, output formats that specify items and their order and handling of blank spaces, and instructions that change prohibitions to affirmatives work together.

Include two or three examples that are relevant, varied, and structured, and surround them with tags to distinguish them from the instructions. The output format includes column names and order, as well as words to use if no values ​​are present. If a ban is absolutely necessary, add a reason and, if possible, change it to something that needs to be done.

Finally, before saving the instructions, preview a few representative inputs to see if they maintain their appearance. If you start writing without checking, you will find it shaking during use. If your follow-up work relies on shape, then shape checking is part of, not the final step in creating instructions.

The three tools do not replace each other, but have different roles. Examples show what it looks like, output formats specify the rules, and positive instructions fill in the gaps left by prohibitions. It is most stable when used together rather than either one alone. This configuration can be copied into ChatGPT's GPT Instructions, Claude Project Instructions, and Gem Instructions in the same way.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The format is not fixed by description alone. When you add examples to the explanation and write down the rules in the blank spaces, it becomes something you can use in subsequent work.

glossary.def: A short pair of inputs and outputs that shows what the desired output should look like. Place two or three items wrapped with tags to distinguish them from the instructions.
It is a framework that determines the items, order, classification method, and blank spaces of the response.
This is a guideline that describes what not to do. The limitation is that it doesn't tell you what to do.
It is a form of sentence that specifically states the action to be taken and its appearance. For example, do not write a description; instead, write that you only print a table.

misconceptions.myth: The longer the prohibited list, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: Prohibition doesn't tell you what to write, so the assistant guesses and fills in the blank spaces. Write down the form of things you need to do first, and only write down the things that are absolutely necessary along with the reasons for prohibitions.
It's easy to follow not only the shape but also the content if you just put in one word. Show me two or three different examples.

misconceptions.myth: The format is fixed as long as it is well explained in words.
misconceptions.fact: Verbal explanations leave room for interpretation. You need to add examples to your explanation to make sure the shape is stable.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Rather than telling you not to do something, it shows you what to do.
Write two or three examples that are relevant, varied, and structured.
The output format includes entry, order, and space rules.
After fixing the format, preview it to make sure it maintains its appearance.

title: Writing examples, output formats, and constraints

checks.q: I included only one completed example in the assistant's instructions for organizing order text, and other orders showed similar items and quantities to that example. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: This is because the examples are ignored because they are not distinct from the guidelines.
This is because if there is only one example, not only the form but also the content is followed.
This is because the order of the output format items is not specified.
This is because this always happens when you wrap an example with tags.
checks.explain: If there is only one example, the assistant will follow the content as well as the shape. If you show two or three different things, only the shape remains.

wrong.0: Even if the examples are separate from the guidelines, they are strongly reflected, so it is not a matter of ignoring them, but of over-following them.
wrong.2: Unspecified order is a problem with item placement being unstable and is not the cause of content being copied.
wrong.3: Wrapping tags is the recommended way to separate instructions from examples.
